items.content: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

You don't need a lot of people to make videos, you need a system, curiosity, desire, and reps. I've done 790 videos since 2021, so at this point it's second nature.

The real trick is I'm not doing this full time. I'm running companies all day, and that's actually where the content comes from. 

I'm taking notes on what I'm learning as I go, and when something's interesting I tell myself to come back and make something out of it. Or I'm in a meeting with someone sharp and I go "you should come on the podcast."

It's not a second job I bolt on, I just made it part of how I already live and work.

items.title: Show HN: FeyNoBg – Automatic background removal model and training library
items.content:
Show HN: FeyNoBg – Automatic background removal model and training library Hey HN, I’m Shreyash from Feyn. We help companies build custom models from their data.

Today, we’re releasing FeyNoBg, an automatic background removal model. Alongside it, we're open-sourcing NoBg, the Python library we built to train and run it.

Try the model here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/feyninc/feynobg. Check out the library here: https://github.com/feyninc/nobg

Some sample outputs:

(1) Soccer Freekick: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MZkAGLwbhNVOZ0Oi7XvpCfSEu9Q...

(2) Hair in wind: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Odc2m0XMVH9uZtvI_KjaRbXzhLL...

(3) Bicycle with visible spokes: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1h99ahjfrtS1MFQJJgiKE2fuM3HZ...

(4) Live Demo video: https://youtu.be/b1heHPvY8BM

Background removal separates an image's subject from its surrounding. We've all tried it at some point. Often it is to reuse the subject in a different artifact. Nowadays, it is common to make chat stickers out of it. It is one of the most common but under-appreciated uses of AI. It is also surprisingly complex. Models can be easily confused by camouflage, motion blur, or fine structures like hair.

The task requires two skills. First, a model has to identify the foreground. Second, it has to trace the foreground’s boundary and estimate an opacity value for each pixel. Generally, these skills are taught with different datasets. That creates a failure point. A poor training mix can improve one skill at the expense of the other. We saw this in our controlled evaluation. A training run with just the MaskFactory dataset improved on the CAMO benchmark but regressed on DIS5K.

For FeyNoBg, we took an interpretability-first approach to training. We first studied how BiRefNet’s stages contribute to finding the foreground and reconstructing its boundary. We discovered that the third stage of it's feature extractor holds a lot of information. Both localization and boundary reconstruction depend heavily on the feature map produced here.

This led us to expand this stage from 18 to 24 blocks while preserving the pre-trained weights. We then trained FeyNoBg on 26.1K diverse examples assembled from 10 datasets. The goal was to improve foreground identification and boundary precision without sacrificing either one.

Across eight benchmarks, FeyNoBg achieves the best published score on four and comes within 2% of the leader on the rest.

Building FeyNoBg also exposed a tooling problem. Image matting models are usually released as isolated repositories with incompatible preprocessing, training, and evaluation code. We built NoBg to solve this. NoBg puts these workflows behind one Python interface. It supports BiRefNet today, with more architectures coming. We hope you build something exciting with it!

Happy to answer any questions!

Anthropic just posted the new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 models.

Master these principles, and Claude instantly becomes 10x smarter.

Here's what changed, and how to apply it to your own setup:

1. Rules → Judgement

Old system prompt said things like "never write multi-line comments." Rigid rules that were sometimes wrong.

New approach: "Write code that reads like the surrounding code."

Newer models have better judgement and don't need to be constrained this hard anymore.

If your CLAUDE.md or skills are full of absolute rules, start testing what happens when you loosen them.

2. Examples → Interface design

Giving Claude examples on how to use a tool actually narrows its exploration space now.

Instead of examples, focus on designing better tool parameters.

Anthropic's own example: labeling a status field as pending/in_progress/completed does more work than an example ever could.

3. Everything upfront → Progressive drip-feeding

Stop cramming every known practice into one giant CLAUDE.md file.

Anthropic moved verification and code review into their own skills that Claude calls only when needed.

Some tools now use deferred loading, meaning Claude has to search for the full definition before using them, so context isn't wasted until it's actually relevant.

Apply this to your own files: build a tree of files loaded at the right time instead of one bloated document.

4. Repetition → Simple tool descriptions

Older models sometimes needed instructions repeated in multiple places to stick. That's no longer true.

Delete the duplicate instructions. Put usage guidance directly in the tool description instead of scattering it across the system prompt too.

5. Manual memory → Auto-memory

You used to have to manually tell Claude to save something to memory.

Claude now automatically saves relevant memories on its own.

6. Simple specs → Rich references

Plain markdown plans are being replaced by richer references: HTML artifacts, actual code, test suites, and even rubrics that let Claude verify against your specific taste in a domain.

A mockup in code will consistently outperform a written description or screenshot of the same thing.

Heres how to adapt and survive AI: 
from someone making $200k/mo at 22 

1. Use your skills to provide a service in the real world.

There are people making $12M per year
with a cleaning company.

Use AI to automate a service business end to end.

A relative of mine makes $140k per month doing this
in a completely different service niche.

2. Build a SaaS which value is not in the code,
but in its network.

A great example of this is @sideshift_app.

Their app is easy to clone,
just like almost any other app is now.

But the network of tens of thousands of creators and companies using their platform is a moat that you cannot clone with Claude.

for example: you can now one-shot Instagram with a single Claude prompt.

But you cannot clone the 1 billion users
that make Instagram worth using. 

3. Build a SaaS that requires special access.

Companies like Postiz or Postbridge require permissions that can sometimes take weeks to acquire.

99.9% people would rather pay you
than fill out all of those applications themselves.

4. Build an app or SaaS for consumers, not founders.

Contrary to what @levelsio and many other indie hackers are saying in this thread of doom about the decline in indie hacker revenue,

our apps revenue has actually grown 7x
in the last two months.

We are growing faster than ever
on all fronts.

Consumerism is at an all-time high,
and it will continue to be for years.

The problem is that Levels and many other indie hackers are selling to people on X 

who are too smart to buy their middle man apps.

Everyone on X knows they can already do this
with one prompt inside of ChatGPT. 

they can probably still thrive if they look for alternative marketing routes outside of X. 

5. I can think of 100 more ways to make money with AI 

→ Agency selling AI services
→ Personal brand 
→ UGC for AI companies that have millions in funding

I mean the list goes on and on. 
And im not just telling you this

i've done most of these businesses and made a 
ton of money on each. 

ultimately my favorite is B2C apps.
because it works the best by far.

don't let this thread scare you into a state of paralisis
And doomer thinking.

levels is speaking from personal experience here. 

Apps and SAAS are very much profitable.

The only adapting you have to do, 

is being a better operator and not 
get stuck on the same channels.

find a solution and keep pushing forward

items.content:
Postiz is still growing by ~$1k/MRR per day ($165k MRR).
You can see proof here: 
https://t.co/AOCjAX5Bg4

I have seen so many B2B SaaS companies losing revenue, and a few that managed to grow past it.

Here is my conclusion, and I might be wrong.
In 2021, when COVID hit, SaaS was booming; tons of indie hackers had high MRR back then that was continuing to grow until 2024.

With AI just available to the public, people made the most generic AI SaaS (mass market). For example, image generators, Video Generators, etc.

But then, there were literally too many people who were doing it, even huge companies like Jasper that raised $100m+

Most of those indies stopped innovating since then.
Usually innovation is not making new features, but actually changing your product or at least your product marketing message.

For example: Postiz changed from a social media scheduling tool to an agent running your social media.
In the main marketing message - not as a feature.

Also, distribution became much harder - hence why people are leaning towards VC money.

Take Higgsfield for example - they are just a Seedance wrapped with an application layer, but their marketing is super aggressive, possible only by funded companies.

So what happened since 2021:
1. "Building in public" was a super interesting thing; everybody wanted to learn about it. Now, it's less effective. You might get tons of views but not many subscriptions.

2. SEO for mass-market products became really hard, as there are tons of those, and it would be really hard to get into the first places on the SERP.

3. Same for ads: more people are bidding, and CAC goes up.

What I think people need to do:
1. Be innovative. One obvious reason is to build for agents because it's easy. If you can implement deep tech, it's also good.

2. Sell the outcome - usually the more niche you get, the easier it is to focus on your use case, so instead of selling "Social media for agents", sell "How to make money by automating your TikTok". Because then people don't buy you because of the software; they buy you because they want to go viral, and that changes the whole mechanism of - everybody can vibe code this.

3. Find other channels to sell it - if you already see that you are failing again and again on X and SEO, you can definitely look for other solutions. Organic content became easier than it was before. Many platforms moved from follower-based to interest-based. You can go viral on TikTok without having a lot of followers. You will have to investigate.

4. Understand the new distribution world - LLMs are now the 1st search engine. How can you rank in AEO? You have to figure it out. And no, it's not just by doing SEO - actually, it can be much, much easier. The most cited websites are Reddit / LinkedIn, and YouTube. Literally, by commenting to people there, LLMs can find you.

5. List yourself in places for distribution - did you know that you can list yourself in the ChatGPT marketplace, Claude marketplace, etc. for both skills and connectors? Postiz already got 2m downloads there.

Final thoughts:
Is it harder? yes.
Is it possible? yes.

If I did it, everybody can do it.

something I keep thinking about after watching that Verona video is this:

almost everyone has experienced a moment where trust became the real problem.

someone sends a payment screenshot.

a seller claims an item has been shipped.

a freelancer says “I already completed the work.”

an account with thousands of followers posts information that turns out to be completely false.

the internet runs on claims, and most of the time we have to decide whether to believe them or not.

that is why @verona_dev makes more sense to me when I stop thinking about it as a blockchain and start thinking about it as proof infrastructure.

in real life, trust is expensive.

businesses hire auditors.

banks run compliance checks.

employers verify certificates.

landlords ask for documents.

all of these processes exist because people can lie, documents can be edited, and screenshots can be faked.

what stood out from the video is that @verona_dev is trying to move that verification process into a system where proof can be checked instead of simply trusted.

and honestly, that feels increasingly relevant in the AI era.

we are entering a world where a fake screenshot takes 30 seconds to create, a cloned voice can sound convincing, and a generated video can spread to millions of people before anyone questions it.

the projects that matter over the next few years may not be the ones creating the most hype.

they may be the ones answering a much simpler question:

“how do we know this is real?”

that is the lens through which I now look at @verona_dev.

not as another token to trade, but as a network being built around a problem that already exists in everyday life:

the growing cost of proving what is true online.

items.content:
how beginners build WEBSITES vs higgsfield ai plugin...

most people treat ai website builders as faster templates. you pick a theme, swap the copy, change the background image, and ship something someone else designed.

the fable 5/claude build works differently because of what's connected to it.

the higgsfield mcp gives claude direct access to nano banana pro and seedance 2.0 during the build. it generates the stills and the video clips itself, in the same session, and drops them straight into the page without downloading assets and reuploading them somewhere else.

having that access changes the order it works in. it produces the images first and writes the code after, because scroll frames get sliced out of visuals that already exist. it figured out that dependency before it started.

the wix tutorial is a beginner level of exactly that. where to click, how to add a section, how to change a background, how to hide an element on mobile. halfway through, it tells you to avoid customizing too much because the design will break. every color in that template was picked to sit next to every other color, so your own taste is a liability inside it. you're editing someone's existing template.

changing an asset after the build is one prompt. the mcp regenerates it, the code updates around it, nothing else in the page moves. inside a template that same change means rebuilding the section.

Just watched @asmartbear teardown @dmytrokrasun's $32k/mo screenshot API (9% churn)

Jason laid out Options A-D:
- Option A: Optimize baseline
- Option B: Build a marketing tool
- Option C: Sell the business
- Option D: Go all-in on MCP / AI

I think Jason missed the best strategy

There’s an "Option E" that is even better 👇

Why not Option D (MCP / AI):

Dmytro noted at 1h:31m that desktop agents already have browser access. Jason brushed it off as a sales objection, but Dmytro is right:

1. Local browsers are free & instant
Cursor, Claude Code, and Windsurf spin up isolated Playwright instances (0ms latency, $0 cost). No 3rd-party API needed for prompts.

2. Static PNGs vs. interactive DOM
Agents don't just need a picture, they click buttons, fill forms, and wait for DOM states. If you need cloud execution, you buy browser infra (@browser_use), not a screenshot API.

3. The "security" argument is backwards
Jason argued local agents get access to "your email and bank". But Playwright launches fresh ephemeral profiles with zero cookies or saved sessions.

Plus, 3rd-party APIs can't reach internal or staging URLs behind a corporate VPN anyway. Local IS the enterprise-safe option.

4. ScreenshotOne’s real moat
It’s not LLM chat prompts, it’s background execution and automation at scale (anti-bot bypass, Cloudflare evasion, 500 parallel renders). That’s how I use it at https://t.co/fiqqEJPjZ6 for web scraping and https://t.co/X5gQf8nHsk for brand identity.

Why Option B (Jason’s version) falls short:

Jason suggested reusing screenshot code for a marketing regression tool, but Dmytro is burned out on screenshots.

The real asset isn't screenshot code. It's DISTRIBUTION.

Dmytro has:
- 1,000 paying B2B customers
- Domain Rating of 62 (DR 62)
- #1 ranking high-intent search traffic

🏆 Option E: Launch SaaS #2 to the same audience

1. Analyze the full workflow
What do users do right before or after screenshots?
- Cold email teams need contact email enrichment
- AI devs need HTML → Clean Markdown for LLMs

Ryan Carson built Treehouse, taught 1M people to code, sold the company, and now runs Untangle as basically a one-person AI startup.

his new skill is not prompting.

it's managing a software factory.

the setup:

> Devon cloud agents instead of local worktrees - 5 to 10 isolated coding environments running at once
> 52-inch monitor with 8 screens open - every agent thread visible like a mini engineering team
> Slack only for agent notifications - the founder becomes the unblocker, not the typist
> 1Password for prod keys - agents never get production write access unless he manually approves it
> phone-first workflow - more than 50% of the company gets managed from mobile
> pinned high-stakes threads - checked every ~25 minutes so the important agents don't drift

the crazy part is the automation layer.

every morning at 9am, a production watchdog scans paid customer activity, summarizes what happened in JSON, and links directly into the admin UI.

then another agent reviews conversations between their AI paralegal “Grace” and real law firm users.

if the score drops below the rubric, it spins up a child coding session and fixes the product.

Ryan says they ship around 3 of these tiny UX fixes per day automatically.

this is the real 2026 skill gap:

most people are still learning how to write better prompts.

the top 1% are learning how to run 10 agents, route tasks between models, protect production, review PRs, and make 20 high-stakes decisions before lunch.

prompt engineering was the tutorial level.

agent management is the job.
